content.text: The text reviews historical concepts, symptoms, pathology, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment of constipation, enteralgia/colic, acute and chronic intestinal catarrh, cholera morbus, and summer diarrhoea/cholera infantum. It emphasizes dietary errors, infection or fermentation, heat, poor sanitation, and constitutional disease. Enteralgia causes recurrent umbilical pain relieved by pressure; catarrh produces diarrhoea, mucus, fever, and inflammation, while severe infantile disease causes vomiting, dehydration, emaciation, and collapse. Management historically centered on rest in bed, dietary regulation, hydration, breast milk or modified cow’s milk, hygiene, cooling, enemata, bismuth, opiates, and selected astringents. Patients were advised to move from crowded cities to cool, dry country, mountain, seaside, or rural locations; New York’s floating hospital carried sick children down the bay for fresh air, and returning them to the city during hot weather was discouraged.
